title: The Effect of Cervical Transcutaneous Vagus Nerve Stimulation on Word Memory in Healthy Adults: A Randomized Single-Blind Study
abstract: Purpose: The noninvasive vagus nerve stimulation has presented a promising adjunctive intervention in cognitive communication disorders. This randomized single-blind study aims to investigate the effect of cervical transcutaneous vagus nerve stimulation (tVNS) on verbal memory in healthy adults. Method: Thirty-one participants were stratified into an experimental group ( n = 22) receiving 30-min cervical tVNS and a control group ( n = 9). Both groups completed a self-paced task to learn 50 Chinese words, followed by an immediate memory test and a 2-week delayed memory test assessing accuracy and reaction time (RT). Data of accuracy and RT were analyzed statistically based on tVNS stimulation, two sessions of memory test, and three age groups. Results: Cervical tVNS significantly improved memory performance, manifested in faster RT and higher accuracy compared to the control group, particularly for young adults. However, accuracy enhancement was age-specific: Only younger adults showed significantly improved recall accuracy with cervical tVNS, while middle-aged and older adults did not. title: Adaptation to Auditory Errors Modulates Perception of the Errors
abstract: Purpose: Speakers adapt to auditory feedback perturbations by modifying their speech output. Although formant-clamp perturbations, in which feedback formants are fixed at predetermined values independent of the speaker's production, demonstrate that adaptation relies on the motor-to-auditory correspondence, it remains unclear how speakers perceive this feedback during adaptation. We hypothesized that if motor adaptation influences perception, then perceptual judgments of experience errors would change alongside adaptation, even when auditory feedback is held constant. Method: Thirty healthy adults performed an adaptation task across four conditions: formant-shift and formant-clamp perturbations, each introduced either suddenly or gradually. During each trial, participants produced consonant–vowel–consonant words and reported their perceived auditory feedback using a continuous vowel-identification slider. We quantified adaptive motor responses during the first 100 ms of the vowel and compared them with perceived errors derived from perceptual reports. title: Shared Variance Across Cognitive Assessments Predicts Language Outcomes in Aphasia: A Preliminary Study
abstract: Purpose: Aphasia, a common consequence of stroke, often co-occurs with cognitive impairments, yet clinical assessment is limited by tools that are lengthy, linguistically demanding, and sometimes redundant. This preliminary study examined shared variance across widely used cognitive tests and explored how the resulting principal components related to aphasia severity and sentence comprehension efficiency. We also tested whether single tasks, those with the strongest component loadings, could predict language outcomes as effectively as the full component scores. Method: Seventeen adults with chronic aphasia and 21 matched controls completed the Test of Everyday Attention, the Cognitive Linguistic Quick Test-Plus, and the Visual and Auditory Duration Attention Network Tests. Principal component analysis (PCA) was used to identify shared variance across cognitive tasks, followed by regression analyses relating components and single-task predictors to language outcomes. title: A Randomized Comparative Effectiveness Trial of Many-Features and Few-Features Variants of Semantic Feature Analysis Treatment for Naming Impairment in Aphasia
abstract: Purpose: Semantic feature analysis (SFA) is a well-established and well-studied treatment for naming impairment in aphasia. Both theory and correlational evidence suggest that feature generation is a key active ingredient of the treatment. The purpose of this study was to test whether the number of features generated by participants in SFA is causally related to outcomes. Method: Forty-one individuals with aphasia due to left-hemisphere stroke of at least 6 months postonset were randomized in a 1:1 ratio to receive either a many-features variant of SFA in which they were asked to generate 11 features per trial or a few-features variant in which they were asked to generate five features per trial. The entire study team, except for three treating clinicians, was blind to group assignment. Random group assignments were stratified by aphasia severity, blocked in groups of four, generated a priori by a team-external consultant, and managed by a treating clinician. title: Automatic Prediction of Vocal Strain Scores in Singing Voice Using Audio and Electroglottographic Modalities
abstract: Purpose: This study developed machine learning models to predict perceptual strain scores in the singing voice using audio and electroglottographic (EGG) recordings. The study examined the predictive capability of distinct feature sets extracted from audio and EGG modalities and assessed the contributions of participant metadata (META) and feature selection to model performance. Method: Data were split into mutually exclusive train-validation ( n = 16 singers, n ≈ 450 samples) and independent test ( n = 11 singers, n ≈ 240 samples) sets to ensure singer-independent generalization. Extracted features included mel-frequency cepstral coefficients, extended Geneva minimalistic acoustic parameter set, wavelet scattering coefficients, and domain-specific descriptors (audio: amplitude modulation; EGG: glottal dynamics), along with singer META. Using leave-one-singer-out cross-validation, we trained regression models (support vector regressor, random forest, and ridge) to predict the expert strain ratings. title: Eye Tracking in Visuoperceptual Diagnostic Tasks in Health Care: A Scoping Review and Thematic Synthesis With Implications for Speech-Language Pathology
abstract: Purpose: Eye tracking provides objective measurement of visuoperceptual behavior during diagnostic interpretation. Although widely used in health care research, little is known about how speech-language pathologists (SLPs) visually engage with dynamic imaging. This scoping review mapped current research on clinicians' gaze behavior during visuoperceptual diagnostic tasks and synthesized methodological trends, outcome themes, and limitations to inform future speech-language pathology–focused eye-tracking research. Method: Following Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses extension for Scoping Reviews guidelines, five databases were searched for studies published between January 2000 and September 2025. Ninety-three studies met inclusion criteria. Data were extracted on study characteristics, diagnostic task characteristics, eye-tracking methodology, gaze outcomes, and reported limitations. Descriptive statistics summarized methodological features, and thematic analysis synthesized outcome trends and barriers. title: Are Bilingual Children With Speech, Language, and Communication Needs More at Risk for Heritage Language Attrition Than Their Typically Developing Peers?
abstract: Purpose: We examined the language environment and proficiency of bilingual children with typical development (TD) and with speech, language, and communication needs (SLCNs). We asked whether the children with SLCNs had more reduced heritage language (HL) experiences than did their TD peers and whether this was associated with a weaker HL and a stronger societal language (SL). Method: Children ( N = 48, M age = 7.89 years) with TD and with SLCNs and their parents participated in this study; all were learning English as their SL with diverse HLs. Parents responded to a detailed questionnaire (Quantifying Bilingual Experience). Children completed a sentence repetition task in English. Results: The SLCN group had more lifetime input and output in the SL than in the HL, but the TD group showed the opposite pattern. The SLCN group had more current SL input and a less rich HL environment than did the TD group. The SLCN group was less willing to use their HL and had lower HL proficiency compared with the TD group. abstract: Purpose: This study examined the impact of clear speech on perceived naturalness. title: Neural Correlates of the Acceptable Noise Level and Self-Reported Listening Skills in Young Adults With Autism Spectrum Disorder
abstract: Purpose: This brain–behavior study investigated the relationship between auditory sensory gating and noise acceptance in listeners with and without autism spectrum disorder (ASD). Relationships between self-reported listening skills and auditory sensory gating were also examined. Method: Neural responses to pure-tone stimuli were elicited using a traditional, passive gating paradigm in 12 listeners with ASD and 12 neurotypical control listeners. Noise acceptance was quantified in all listeners using the acceptable noise level (ANL) measure. Self-reported listening abilities were measured using the Speech, Spatial, and Qualities of Hearing Scale (SSQ). Relationships between neural and behavioral measures were analyzed using linear mixed-effects regression. Results: Listeners with ASD accepted less noise when listening to concurrent speech, had higher intensity most comfortable levels for speech, and reported significantly more difficulties on the SSQ compared to the control group. title: Multimodal Language Processing in Children With Developmental Language Disorder: The Influence of Verbal and Visuospatial Memory
abstract: Purpose: This study investigates how verbal and visuospatial memory capacities contribute to the processing and comprehension of pragmatic meanings that are expressed multimodally in children with and without developmental language disorder (DLD). Method: Seventy-seven children (33 with DLD, 44 typically developing [TD]), aged 5–10 years, completed standardized memory tasks and participated in a visual-world eye-tracking experiment assessing both online processing and offline comprehension of sentences with simple and complex pragmatic meanings (interrogativity and indirect requests, respectively). Sentences were presented under three conditions: baseline (no prosodic nor gestural cues to target meanings), prosodically enhanced (target meanings enhanced through prosodic cues), and multimodally enhanced (target meanings enhanced through prosodic and gestural cues). Results: In accordance with previous findings, children with DLD showed significantly lower verbal and visuospatial memory scores than their TD peers, with more pronounced difficulties in the verbal domain. title: Acoustic and Perceptual Speech Production Differences in Preschoolers With a History of Late and Typical Talking
abstract: Purpose: While an emerging body of research has demonstrated that late talkers (LTs) show continued subclinical deficits in language abilities, less is known about their development of speech production skills. The current study investigated speech production abilities among 3-year-old children with a history of late talking (hLTs) or typical talking (hTTs) using three measures of speech production skills. Method: We assessed speech production skills in a sample of 3-year-old children who were previously identified as LTs or typical talkers (44 hTTs, 31 hLTs) using a norm-referenced assessment of articulation abilities, a caregiver-report measure of speech intelligibility, and fine-grained acoustic analyses of both earlier- and later-acquired speech contrasts. We compared groups using continuous measures of performance. Results: Across all three measurement methods/types, hLTs showed poorer speech production skills compared to hTTs. title: Characterizing the Speech Breathing Kinematics of Older Adults With Presbyphonia
abstract: Background: Age-related changes to laryngeal and respiratory systems contribute to presbyphonia, yet the speech breathing behaviors that accompany or exacerbate ageing voice problems remain poorly characterized. This study examined speech breathing kinematics in older adults with presbyphonia and compared them with published data from vocally healthy peers. Method: Thirty-five adults with presbyphonia (20 men, 15 women; M age = 79.8 years) completed reading and monologue tasks in comfortable and background noise conditions while inductive plethysmography and calibrated acoustics were recorded. Primary outcome was lung volume initiation (LVI) expressed as % vital capacity (%VC) relative to end-expiratory level. title: The Effect of Between-Ear Speech Perception Asymmetry on Localization, Spoken Language, and Literacy for Adolescents With Cochlear Implants
abstract: Purpose: This study aimed to examine the effects of between-ear speech perception asymmetry on localization, spoken language, and reading in adolescents with early cochlear implants (CIs). Method: Eighty adolescents, who have long-term bilateral device use, participated: 10 with bimodal (BM) devices (CI plus hearing aid at the nonimplanted ear) and 70 with bilateral CIs (BCIs; 14 simultaneous, 56 sequential). Participants completed localization, unilateral speech perception, receptive language, and reading tests. Principal component analysis created composite scores for better-ear speech perception and between-ear speech perception asymmetry. Hierarchical regression examined the effects of demographics, audiological factors, and asymmetry on outcomes. Results: Localization scores for the two BCI groups did not differ significantly. title: Effect of Vowel Type on Aerodynamic Measures of Estimated Subglottal Pressure and Airflow
abstract: Introduction: The purpose of this study was to investigate the potential effect of factors such as tongue height and advancement and vocal tract constrictions on aerodynamic measures of voice (mean airflow [MAF] and estimated subglottal pressure [Psub]). A key question was whether the choice of elicitation vowel would have a substantial impact on normative expectations and subsequent clinical decision making that may be based on measures of MAF or Psub. Method: Forty-three nondysphonic male ( n = 13) and female ( n = 30) participants between the ages of 18 and 30 years were tested using the Phonatory Aerodynamic System (Model 6600, Pentax Medical Inc.). title: Contribution of Phonological Information to Lexical Access in School-Age Children With Cochlear Implants
abstract: Purpose: This study explores the interplay of phonological and lexical processing in children, focusing on whether German-speaking school-age children with cochlear implants (CIs) use phonological information for lexical access in the same way as their peers with typical hearing (TH). The study aimed at understanding how different phonological contrasts between a target and a phonological competitor affect lexical access when this acoustic information is less available, as is the case with CIs. Method: Using an eye-tracking visual-world paradigm, we hypothesized that lexical access would differ for the children with CIs due to their shorter hearing experience and/or the characteristics of the auditory input provided by the implants. We further hypothesized that processing the difference between a target and its phonological competitor would depend on the types and number of contrasting features available. title: Predictors of Word Learning With and Without Retrieval Practice in Children With Developmental Language Disorder
abstract: Purpose: Both children with developmental language disorder (DLD) and their peers with typical language development (TD) vary in their response to word learning activities, even when a consistent procedure is used. In this study, we examine child factors that might help explain this variation in outcomes and whether any interaction between these factors operates in the same way as a function of whether retrieval practice is included in the word learning procedure. Method: We examined the relations between a common set of child factors and children's responses in five previously published novel word learning studies with similar procedures. Participants were 4- and 5-year-old English-speaking children with DLD and their same-age peers with TD. Factors included scores on standardized language and nonverbal intelligence tests, nonword repetition, maternal education, age, and group status (TD, DLD). title: Neural Indicators of Inhibition in Tinnitus: Onset–Offset and Sensory Gating Auditory Evoked Potentials Vary by Stimulus Frequency and Tinnitus Severity
abstract: Purpose: The purpose of this study was to evaluate the effect of stimulus frequency and tinnitus severity on measurements indicative of inhibition called onset–offset and sensory gating auditory evoked potentials (AEPs). The specific aims were to (a) determine the effect of stimulus frequency on AEPs in people with and without tinnitus; (b) determine if people with high-frequency tinnitus demonstrate abnormal AEPs in response to high-frequency stimuli; and (c) compare AEPs in people with tinnitus of varying severity. Method: A total of 26 people with tinnitus and 26 age-, sex-, and hearing-matched no-tinnitus controls participated. AEPs were recorded in response to stimuli of varying frequency (broadband noise [BBN], 0.25, 2, 8 kHz). AEPs were quantified by measuring difference wave amplitudes and latencies. For Aims 1 and 2, mixed-model ANOVAs were calculated to determine the main effect of and interaction between stimulus frequency and tinnitus presence. title: Characterizing Submental Neuromuscular Activity of Swallowing Rehabilitation: An Electromyographic Evaluation of Rehabilitative Maneuvers in Healthy Adults
abstract: Purpose: The effortful swallow (ES), the Mendelsohn maneuver (MM), and isometric tongue presses (TPs) are widely used swallowing maneuvers/exercises to improve elements of swallowing, such as muscle strength and biomechanics. However, the underlying neuromuscular mechanisms of these exercises remain unclear, potentially limiting our ability to specify treatment targets and improve treatment efficacy. This study aimed to compare submental neuromuscular activation patterns during the ES, MM, TPs, and typical swallows in healthy young and older adults. Method: As part of a larger randomized crossover validation study, 60 healthy adults (30 young and 30 older) completed typical swallows and three maneuvers using a wearable submental surface electromyographic (sEMG) system (i-Phagia). title: Characterizing Caregiver–Child Interactions Through a Transactional Lens: A Baseline Analysis of a Caregiver-Implemented Intervention
abstract: Purpose: This study was motivated by the transactional model of development and examined the reciprocal influences that children and caregivers have on caregiver–child interactions (CCXs) prior to a caregiver-implemented intervention. We tested whether child communication characteristics were associated with caregiver strategy use and whether these strategies, in turn, influenced children's communication to understand how caregivers and children mutually shaped the language learning environment. Method: Caregiver–child dyads ( N = 105) were participants in a randomized controlled trial. CCXs were collected when children were approximately 30 months of age, transcribed, and coded for four caregiver language facilitation strategies and child communication variables. title: Explanatory Sequential Mixed-Methods Study of the Effectiveness of the Childhood Dysphagia Management Scale (CDMS): Part 2 of a CDMS Hybrid Effectiveness–Implementation Study
abstract: Purpose: As Part 2 of a Type 1 hybrid effectiveness–implementation study, we evaluated the effectiveness of the Childhood Dysphagia Management Scale (CDMS), a validated pediatric dysphagia outcomes assessment completed by therapists following instrumental swallow assessments. Method: Guided by the Reach, Effectiveness, Adoption, Implementation, and Maintenance and Consolidated Framework for Implementation Research implementation science frameworks, mixed methods were used to evaluate CDMS effectiveness in a tertiary care children's hospital system across the following areas: general/workflow, referrals, follow-up care, communication, and patient/caregiver impact. Using an explanatory sequential design, quantitative results informed qualitative interview guides. journal_name: Journal of Speech, Language & Hearing Research
title: Academic English Language Screeners: Gatekeepers for Multilingual Learners
abstract: Purpose: This article describes the gatekeeping nature of academic English language screeners for multilingual learners. It highlights inequities in current English learner identification practices, advocates for universal academic language screening, and emphasizes the need for teacher training to support academic language development for all students, regardless of home language background. Conclusion: The article argues that more equitable and comprehensive identification practices, paired with strengthened teacher training, are essential to ensure that all students receive appropriate language support and are not disadvantaged by current screening systems.

title: Neural Processing of Phoneme Changes: Differences Between Children and Adults
abstract: Purpose: This study examined neural differences in processing of phoneme changes between 5- and 6-year-old Chinese–English bilingual young children and adults using a passive oddball task and event-related potentials. Method: Natural speech stimuli with digital refinement were used. Two syllables differing in vowels were manipulated: /da/ (the standard) and /di/ (the deviant). Results: The mismatch negativity (MMN) and P3a were elicited by /di/ relative to /da/ in both the young child and adult groups. However, young children showed a reduced MMN, indicated by smaller mean amplitudes and later peak latencies, compared with adults, although peak-amplitude differences were not statistically significant. Young children also exhibited a significantly enhanced P3a (both mean amplitude and peak amplitude) alongside a delayed peak latency relative to adults. Notably, young children elicited a robust late mismatch response, manifesting as a significant positivity, whereas adults showed no significant response. title: Lexical Bias During Speech Perception Increases Under Signal Degradation but Not Cognitive Load
abstract: Purpose: Lexical information shapes the interpretation of ambiguous speech sounds, often biasing perception toward real words rather than nonwords—a phenomenon known as lexical bias. This study examined the extent to which signal degradation and cognitive load modulate this bias. Method: Younger adults with normal hearing categorized stimuli along two word–nonword continua (Bap/Gap and Back/Gack), which differed primarily in the formant transitions of the initial consonant. Stimuli were either unprocessed or vocoded to introduce signal degradation, simulating cochlear implant listening. Cognitive load was manipulated via a dual-task paradigm: Participants memorized digits (Experiment A) or images (Experiment B) under low- and high-cognitive-load conditions while performing the categorization task. title: Low-Intensity Distortion Product Otoacoustic Emission Protocols in Infants and Young Children: Contributions of Age-Specific Ear Characteristics
abstract: Purpose: Despite almost complete cochlear maturity at birth, distortion product otoacoustic emission (DPOAE) levels in neonates and infants are typically higher than those measured in older children and adults, depending on the type and frequency stimulus, which suggests functional immaturity of the cochlea as well as the role of the outer and/or middle ear. This study aimed to investigate the relationship between outer and middle ear characteristics, using wideband tympanometry (WBT), and DPOAEs and to evaluate the applicability of normative criteria at reduced stimulus intensities in children aged between 6 days and 5 years. Method: A total of 109 ears from 60 participants were examined and categorized into three age groups: newborns, infants (6–8 months), and children (3–5 years). The following measurements were analyzed: ear canal volume, compensated acoustic admittance (with 1-kHz probe tone and 226-Hz probe tone), acoustic absorbance, and DPOAEs with two stimulus intensity protocols ( L 1 – L 2 = 65–55 and 55–45 dB SPL). Statistical analyses included nonparametric tests and correlation models. Results: WBT measures reflect the age-related maturation of the conductive pathway.

title: Connecting Preschoolers' Spontaneous Speech Patterns to Future Language Skills: A 3-Year Concurrent and Longitudinal Cohort Study of Canonical Proportion as a Developmental Index
abstract: Purpose: Understanding how children's spontaneous language behavior relates to standardized metrics of speech and language remains a crucial challenge in studies of language acquisition and clinical assessment. Traditional lab- and clinic-based paradigms are time- and resource-intensive and may not fully capture a child's underlying language competencies. This study aimed to investigate whether automated analysis of naturalistic, child-centered audio recordings can index the developmental trajectory of speech-language abilities from 2 to 5 years of age. Method: A longitudinal design was employed with N = 155 preschoolers, who were followed from 2 to 5 years of age. Deep learning speech classification methods were used to compute canonical proportion—the proportion of a child's speech that is produced as canonical syllables (well-formed syllables with a consonant–vowel transition, such as “ba”), a key marker of speech motor control development and phonological representation building—from child-centered audio recordings collected at 2–4 years of age. title: Short-Term Neurobehavioral Effects of Acute Respiratory Illness on Auditory–Motor Integration During Speech Production
abstract: Purpose: COVID-19 is an acute respiratory illness that has been shown to impair speech and voice, yet its effects on the neural dynamics of speech production remain largely unknown. This longitudinal study investigated the short-term neurobehavioral impact of COVID-19 on sensorimotor control of speech production. Method: Before and after COVID-19 infection, participants in the experimental group produced sustained vowels while hearing their voice unexpectedly pitch-shifted in auditory feedback. An age- and sex-matched control group without intervening COVID-19 infection underwent identical testing across a comparable interval. Vocal compensations and event-related potentials (ERPs), together with source localization and Granger causality analyses, were used to characterize the neurobehavioral effects of COVID-19 on vocal feedback control. title: Efficient Language Sampling for Deaf and Hard of Hearing Children: Evaluating Reliability Across Length, Timing, and Context
abstract: Purpose: Given the time demands of language sample analysis, this study aimed to identify efficient, flexible sampling procedures that maintain strong reliability. We examine how language sample length in minutes, timing (i.e., beginning vs. later in the elicitation task following a warm-up period), and elicitation context (i.e., play or conversation) influence the reliability of four common language measures in young deaf and hard of hearing (DHH) children. Method: Participants included 21 DHH children (3–5 years old) who completed 10-min play and conversation samples in English. Samples were transcribed and analyzed for mean length of utterance in words, mean length of utterance in morphemes, total number of words per minute, and number of different words per minute. We evaluated the reliability of these measures by comparing shorter segments (i.e., 1, 3, 5, and 7 min) to the full sample using Cronbach's alpha, with additional comparisons based on the sample's timing and elicitation context. title: Fundamental Frequency and Noise Effects on Sentence Recognition in Mandarin-Speaking Autistic Children: The Role of Cognitive Abilities
abstract: Purpose: Previous studies have shown that Mandarin-speaking autistic children exhibit atypical pitch processing and their speech perception is easily affected by noise. This study examined how fundamental frequency ( F 0) contour and background noise affect Mandarin sentence recognition in autistic children, and evaluated the roles of verbal intelligence (VIQ), nonverbal intelligence (NVIQ), and working memory (WM) as cognitive predictors. Method: Thirty Mandarin-speaking autistic children and 31 age-matched typically developing (TD) controls completed an open-set sentence recognition task under four conditions: natural F 0 (NF0) versus flat F 0 (FF0) in quiet and in speech-shaped noise at 10 dB SNR. Performance was scored as percent correct monosyllables. VIQ and NVIQ were assessed using the Wechsler Intelligence Scale, and WM was assessed via forward digit span. title: Interactive Effects of Executive Function and Language Ability on Children's Cross-Situational Word Learning
abstract: Purpose: This study examined whether executive function (EF) skills predict cross-situational word learning (CSWL) in children and whether EF–CSWL relationships vary as a function of language ability, including in children with developmental language disorder (DLD). Method: Fifty monolingual English-speaking children 5–9 years of age completed a CSWL task in which they learned five novel words. title: Multi-Atlas–Based Segmentation of Pediatric Vocal Tract Anatomy in Dynamic Magnetic Resonance Imaging
abstract: Purpose: Segmentation of velopharyngeal and vocal tract anatomy is crucial for quantifying structures and analyzing dynamics during speech. title: Adolescents Activate Phonology When Reading Familiar Words
abstract: Purpose: A central debate in reading research is how phonology functions in written word recognition. title: Development of the Receptive and Expressive Vocabulary of Children in Different Care Settings: A Longitudinal Exploration
abstract: Purpose: Language development in children is influenced by both environmental and individual factors. This study examined vocabulary development among children in care, longitudinally considering environmental (different care types) and individual (temperament) factors. title: Conversational–Communicative Experience and Theory of Mind in Taiwanese Deaf and Hard of Hearing Children
abstract: Purpose: This study examined theory-of-mind (ToM) development in Taiwanese deaf and hard of hearing (DHH) children with early hearing provisions, extending prior evidence from Western contexts. title: Does the Presence of Semantic Head Facilitate Novel Word Learning in Mandarin-Speaking Children?
abstract: Purpose: Characteristics of to-be-learned words influence word learning but are understudied in Mandarin-speaking children. title: Domains of Psychosocial Risk in School-Aged Cochlear Implant Users
abstract: Purpose: The purpose of this study was to identify domains of psychosocial risk specific to school-aged cochlear implant (CI) users and to explain individual differences in psychosocial risk within the CI sample. title: Reading Comprehension and Orthographic Consistency: Modeling Direct and Indirect Pathways in Children With Reading Difficulties
abstract: Purpose: This study examined how orthographic transparency shapes reading comprehension (RC) among third-grade students with reading difficulties (RD). title: Factors Influencing Auditory Perception of Masculinity and Naturalness in Transmasculine Voices
abstract: Purpose: This study examined speaker- and listener-related factors that influence auditory perception of masculinity, naturalness, and gender attribution in transmasculine voices on hormone replacement therapy and in cisgender speakers. title: Dose Considerations and Generalization Following Script Training for Poststroke Aphasia: A Randomized Factorial Clinical Trial

abstract: Purpose: This study aimed to investigate whether Chinese children with dyslexia exhibit atypical left-hemispheric beta/gamma oscillatory patterns during nonverbal auditory processing and to examine whether phonological skills mediate the relationship between these oscillations and reading ability. title: Consonant Articulating Errors in Khmer-Speaking Preschool Children: A Picture-Naming Task Analysis
abstract: Purpose: Consonant errors (mainly phonetic and phonological errors) as a phenomenon in speech development are frequently observed in preschool children's daily speech communication across languages. title: Implementation of Communication Disability Documentation and Accommodations in Primary Care: A Pragmatic Type III Hybrid Implementation-Effectiveness Trial Protocol
abstract: Purpose: Routine collection of patients' communication disability (CD) status is instrumental for monitoring and addressing health disparities, including the provision of disability accommodations. title: Family Media Exposure and Caregiver-Reported Child Language Profiles
abstract: Purpose: This study described media exposure patterns of adults and children aged 0–5 years and examined associations among quantity, types, and context of media exposure and caregiver descriptions of child language. Method: Participants were 170 caregivers, primarily mothers with graduate degrees and high socioeconomic status, representing 244 children. abstract: Purpose: The aims of this study were to subjectively and quantitatively analyze vocal tremor (VT) in patients with adductor laryngeal dystonia (ADLD) using video feature tracking of stroboscopic laryngoscopy recordings, to observe the VT incidence and characterize tremor directionality and kinematic parameters, and to identify differences between the patients with intermittent dystonia tremor (iDT) and regular dystonia tremor (rDT). abstract: Purpose: Clinical trials provide essential evidence for determining whether interventions are safe, effective, clinically meaningful, and suitable for translation into practice. title: Unraveling Individual Second-Language Acquisition in Late Bilingual Children With and Without Suspected Developmental Language Disorder: A Longitudinal Approach
abstract: Purpose: Research in bilingual language acquisition has experienced a shift toward more individual-focused analyses within longitudinal studies. abstract: Purpose: Self-perception of voice is a critical outcome for individuals seeking gender-affirming care; however, the variables associated with vocal self-perception remain unclear. abstract: Purpose: Broad linguistic properties of masker speech (e.g., phonological and prosodic familiarity) have been shown to affect target speech transcription during speech-on-speech listening. abstract: Purpose: The purpose of this study was to identify and describe extrapulmonary cough receptors located in healthy individuals' larynges and pharynges and the types of stimuli to which they are sensitive. abstract: Purpose: This study aimed to evaluate the evidence on speech perception abilities of children with speech sound disorders (SSDs) to understand how the perceptual skills contribute to the diagnosis and characterization of SSDs. abstract: Purpose: Auditory and somatosensory systems jointly support vocal motor control, yet their relative contributions in primary muscle tension dysphonia (pMTD) remain poorly understood. abstract: Purpose: Developmental language disorder (DLD) has been associated with difficulties in several cognitive and emotional domains, including emotion recognition (ER). title: Linguistically Informed Automated Estimates of Creak in Adductor Laryngeal Dystonia
abstract: Purpose: Creaky voice is a perceptually low-pitched and irregular voice quality that has shown promise as an objective marker of adductor laryngeal dystonia (AdLD). title: Phonological Awareness and Reading Impairments in Cantonese Speakers With Congenital Amusia: Comorbid Dyslexia Traits Matter
abstract: Purpose: This study investigated the nature and underlying mechanisms of phonological awareness and literacy impairments in Cantonese-speaking adults with congenital amusia (amusia hereafter) while accounting for the potential role of dyslexia traits. Method: Twenty-one Cantonese speakers with amusia and 21 matched controls were assessed using segmental (onset phoneme deletion and spoonerism) and suprasegmental (tone oddity) phonological awareness tasks, literacy tasks (word reading, 1-min word reading, and dictation), and auditory perception threshold tasks (pitch discrete, pitch glide, and rise time). title: Lessons From the Communication Bridge Trials: Advancing Meaningful Dyadic Interventions Toward Implementation
abstract: Purpose: This review describes the historical motivations, development, and evolution of the Communication Bridge (CB) research program, which is designed to maximize quality of life and minimize burden for individuals living with dementia and their communication partners. The CB trials described comprise a series of dyadic, nonpharmacologic interventions supporting individuals with primary progressive aphasia (PPA) and their communication partners. title: Kinematic Features of Laryngeal Motor Control in Parkinson's Disease
abstract: Purpose: Laryngeal kinematics were examined under high-speed videoendoscopy to examine laryngeal motor control of persons with Parkinson's disease (PD). title: Early Organization of Simultaneous Multimodal Behaviors: Perception- and Production-Based Contingencies as a Scaffold for Language Development
abstract: Aim: This study investigated how infants' simultaneous multimodal behaviors (SMBs)—the concurrent coordination of vocal, gaze, facial, and manual signals—are organized during natural caregiver–infant interactions at 3 and 6 months. title: Verbal Mediation During Shifting in School-Aged Children With Developmental Language Disorder
abstract: Purpose: Children with developmental language disorder (DLD) often exhibit deficits in executive function. These deficits may be linked to less effective verbal mediation or the use of self-directed language to guide task performance. This study examined the role of verbal mediation during an executive shifting task. Method: Twenty-seven children aged 8–12 years (15 with DLD, 12 with typical development [TD]) completed a cued local–global task with verbal mediation (baseline) and without (articulatory suppression). title: Hearing Aid Benefit in Auditory Neuropathy Due to Friedreich Ataxia: A Case Report
abstract: Purpose: Friedreich ataxia is one of the most common recessively inherited ataxias, with hearing loss due to auditory neuropathy being a recognized complication. However, there are limited data on the best interventions for hearing loss in these patients. We report the significant behavioral and subjective benefits of binaural amplification in a patient with auditory neuropathy due to Friedreich ataxia. title: Intelligibility of Emotional Speech in Chinese Older Adults: Effects of Age-Related Hearing Loss
abstract: Purpose: The intelligibility of speech with emotional prosody may decline with aging and hearing loss. This study examined the effects of aging and age-related hearing loss on word recognition for Mandarin words spoken with different emotional prosodies. title: Respiratory–Swallow Training in Head and Neck Cancer: Impact on Swallowing Safety and Efficiency
abstract: Purpose: This review article provides a programmatic translational synthesis of a research program investigating respiratory–swallow coordination as a modifiable physiologic target underlying swallowing impairment and safety, with a focus on individuals treated for head and neck cancer (HNC). The purpose is to synthesize physiologic evidence, clinical trial outcomes, and translational advances supporting respiratory–swallow training (RST) as a mechanism-based intervention. title: Dissociable Effects of Dysarthria Etiology and Severity on the Minimally Detectable Change of Speech Intelligibility
abstract: Purpose: The minimally detectable change (MDC) provides a threshold for interpreting changes in outcome measures that are outside of measurement error. There is emerging evidence that dysarthria etiology and speech severity impact the MDC of speech intelligibility; however, an investigation of these factors is needed to determine the unique effects of dysarthria etiology and speech severity. The purpose of the current study was to calculate and compare MDCs of speech intelligibility across five dysarthria etiology groups and four severity levels. title: Clinical Reasoning Under Uncertainty in Speech-Language Pathology When Measures, Labels, and Best-Practice Claims Get Ahead of Evidence
abstract: Purpose: Speech-language pathologists often have to make consequential decisions with evidence that is incomplete, indirect, or mixed. The risk is not uncertainty itself, but the way an indirect measure, a familiar label, or a best-practice statement can begin to carry more interpretive weight than it can support. This tutorial focuses on the point where observations are turned into claims and claims are turned into recommendations. Method: The tutorial draws on scholarship in measurement and assessment showing that a score or result only has meaning through how it is interpreted and how it is used in practice. abstract: Purpose: This meta-analysis aimed to compare the performance of deaf and hard of hearing (DHH) children who use cochlear implants (CIs) or hearing aids (HAs) with their typically hearing (TH) peers on false belief (FB) understanding tasks. title: Comprehension of Restrictive Focus With Zing6hai6 (“Only”) in School-Age Cantonese-Speaking Autistic and Neurotypical Children
abstract: Purpose: This study investigated the comprehension of restrictive focus with the focus particle zing6hai6 (“only”) in school-age Cantonese-speaking autistic and neurotypical children. title: From Underrepresentation to Inclusion: Women Who Stutter in Research and Practice
abstract: Purpose: Women who stutter have historically received limited analytic attention in stuttering research and clinical practice. Although the higher male-to-female persistence ratio partly shapes sample composition, repeated reliance on male-majority samples has also contributed to a sex-skewed evidence base, limiting insight into women's experiences and clinical needs. Using a biopsychosocial framework, this article identifies key domains for inquiry and proposes a research, clinical, and educational agenda to address the underrepresentation of women who stutter and its implications for evidence generation, care, and professional training. title: Reliability and Validity of the Mandarin Articulation and Phonological Test: Scale Development and Psychometric Properties for Preschool Children
abstract: Purpose: This study aimed to (a) develop preliminary reference data for the Mandarin Articulation and Phonological Test (MAPT) and (b) examine its reliability and validity for assessing speech abilities in Mandarin-speaking preschool children aged 3–6 years. title: Chirp-Evoked Electrocochleography and Speech-in-Noise Performance in Normal-Hearing Individuals With Tinnitus
abstract: Purpose: Both tinnitus and poor hearing-in-noise performance have been proposed as perceptual consequences of cochlear synaptopathy, which can occur in the absence of significant hearing loss. title: Age and Discourse Task Independently Influence Disfluency Production
abstract: Purpose: Aging is often associated with increased difficulty in speech production (e.g., increased word-finding difficulties and disfluencies), as well as with broader cognitive changes such as declines in executive function (EF) and greater sensitivity to task constraints. title: The Validity, Reliability, and Accuracy of the European French Version of the Intelligibility in Context Scale
abstract: Purpose: The Intelligibility in Context Scale (ICS) is a free parent report questionnaire assessing functional intelligibility. Although it has been translated into French, it lacks validation. This study addresses two main objectives. abstract: Purpose: Measuring language proficiency in the presence of nonmainstream dialect variation is a crucial task for clinicians and language researchers. abstract: Purpose: This study aimed to translate, culturally adapt, and preliminarily evaluate the Mandarin version of the Hearing and Functioning in Everyday Life Questionnaire (HFEQ-Mandarin) for older adults with hearing loss. abstract: Purpose: Sleep plays a critical role in speech-sound learning. abstract: Purpose: Imitation and language are associated in autistic children. However, imitation involves various types. This cross-sectional study examined the associations between different imitation abilities and receptive and expressive language skills in autistic preschoolers while controlling for nonverbal IQ (NVIQ). abstract: Purpose: Differences in the size of velopharyngeal structures across racial groups at rest have been described in the literature, with race influencing adenoid thickness, pharyngeal depth, effective velar length, and velar length. abstract: Purpose: The purpose of this study was to develop and test standardized stimuli for the Pediatric Auditory-Perceptual Evaluation of Voice protocol. abstract: Purpose: The purpose of this study was to investigate the relationship between orthographic transcription and visual analog scale (VAS) intelligibility ratings across read and spontaneous speech in speakers with Parkinson's disease (PD), speakers with multiple sclerosis (MS), and healthy controls. abstract: Purpose: Although auditory-perceptual voice assessments are crucial for evaluating pediatric voices, no protocol designed for use with children has been established. abstract: Purpose: This study examined whether phoneme-level posterior probabilities generated by an articulatory-informed deep learning model (Phonet) can serve as interpretable and sensitive markers of articulatory impairment in motor speech disorders (MSDs).
